title: Royal Bank of Canada, 2016 BresciaLEAD Distinction Award Recipient
description: On Thursday, April 7, 2016 over 740 guests gathered at the London Convention Centre to celebrate today's generation of outstanding women leaders at the inaugural BresciaLEAD Awards.   The Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) was selected as the recipient of the Distinction Award for being an organization that values the unique and diverse contributions that women leaders and women's leadership weave into their organizational fabric.

asr.full_text: Diversity and inclusion is one of our core values at RBC and for decades we've had a real focus on the advancement of women and I think the key goals that we have are around representation on our board, so starts at the top. We're very proud today to have our chair be a woman, it's about representation in executive ranks and we are proud to also have made good progress there and we're at 39% of our executives and then our senior leadership and and leadership roles in general, because still, 62% of our population are women. So, we have a real focus on making sure that women feel they have the tools and support they need to advance in their careers. You know, I think when it comes to diversity and inclusion, and this doesn't just apply to women, I think it's absolutely critical that as a large service organization serving clients that we represent those that we serve and obviously with the population of business owners the fastest growing segment of business owners is women and so it would be a smart not just a right thing to do, but also a smart thing to do to be able to make sure that we represent the full spectrum of those that we represent in our ranks. Unconscious bias, I believe, has really been at the root of why women might not have moved ahead. People were thinking, while they might not have moved ahead. People were thinking while they might not have been saying well, they're in childbearing years, maybe they're going to take some time off, and I think it's really important to get those kind of things out on the table. and so what I believe Unconscious Bias has done and the discussion about Unconscious Bias has started at the top. We have our Diversity Leadership Council chaired by our CEO and these are the discussions that they have around that table where there's representation from all businesses is to say, how do we make sure those issues get out on the table so that they're not unconscious and they're conscious and if they're conscious, you can actually do something about them. I think my favourite group to talk to are young and emerging leaders, particularly women. Because I think that I did an article this week about the confidence gap, and I think often it holds us back as women. You know, there are studies that say that women wait until they can tick 100 percent of the boxes before they apply for a job, where a man might only tick 50 percent, and he'll go for it and he'll go for it hard. And so I think that women, young women in particular, need to have the confidence to know that they will learn from every job and that they're not going to know everything when they go into new roles. And it's important to take risks early in their career to learn as much as they possibly can across a wide spectrum of things so then their tool kit is really well developed as they come to compete for more senior roles. So I think a key piece of advice would be to take some chances, develop a network of people that you trust that will give you honest feedback about how you're doing.
